steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on using pure dual-encoder models for extreme multi-label classification (XMC). It should contrast XMC with open-domain QA retrieval, question the belief that dual encoders alone aren't enough, introduce our loss functions and scaling approach, and end with a contributions list and a roadmap of the paper.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Dual encoders in openQA dense retrieval; nature of openQA training data
- Many-shot retrieval framed as XMC; memorize vs. generalize
- Prevailing belief that DE alone is not enough; synthetic memorization experiment
- Research question: are pure DE sufficient? Why pure DE is desirable; DEXML results
- Loss analysis, proposed losses, scaling to all negatives
- Contributions and paper roadmap

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- DE in openQA dense retrieval
  - DE very successful for dense retrieval in openQA systems
  - retrieve relevant passages/documents from large corpus given a query
  - map queries + documents into shared embedding space -> fast similarity search
  - openQA benchmarks: multi-class (most queries have a single positive doc), limited data (each doc zero/very few tagged queries, zero/few-shot)
  - so models must generalize to documents that may not appear in training set
- Many-shot retrieval = XMC
  - real-world apps: search engines, recommendation systems
  - retrieve multiple documents/items from large collection, many seen examples per item (many-shot)
  - formulated as XMC, each document/item = separate label
  - also RAG: when multiple documents may contain the answer, RAG retrieval ~ XMC
  - XMC needs to "memorize" and "generalize"
  - e.g. product to product recommendation: memorize which products lead to click on a product, from product-product co-click data; still generalize to unseen queries
- Belief: DE not sufficient for XMC
  - reason: semantic gap, knowledge-intensive benchmarks
  - SOTA XMC methods augment DE with per-label classifiers or auxiliary parameters
  - our synthetic test: random query text paired with random document text, memorize the random correlations
  - DE gets perfect accuracy up to 1M scale (Section C.1) -> disputes belief
- Question: "Are pure DE models sufficient for XMC tasks?"
  - pure DE desirable: 1) parameter efficient, model size / trainable params don't scale linearly with #labels (Figure 1); 2) XMC methods need re-training/updates for new labels, DE generalize to new labels via features
  - result: pure DE match or beat SOTA XMC by up to 2% on largest public benchmarks, 20 \times smaller
  - key: right loss formulation + extensive negatives for consistent, unbiased loss feedback
  - name: DEXML (Dual-Encoders for eXtreme Multi-Label classification)
- Losses and scaling
  - analyze OvA-BCE and InfoNCE: OvA-BCE doesn't train effectively, InfoNCE disincentivizes confident predictions
  - \mathsf{DecoupledSoftmax}: simple modification of InfoNCE, removes correlation between positive labels
  - {\mathsf{SoftTop}\text{-k}}: optimize accuracy within prediction budget size (k); fixed number of highly accurate predictions
  - long tail of labels -> many highly relevant negatives per query -> first study loss with all negatives
  - all negatives hard at million-label scale -> memory-efficient distributed implementation, multiple GPUs, modified gradient cache; modest GPU setup (Table 1, 9)
  - also approximations via standard hard negative mining
- Contributions + roadmap
  - DE alone reach SOTA on XMC; parameter-efficient, generalizable; unifies XMC and retrieval
  - existing losses not appropriate (OvA-BCE, InfoNCE)
  - DecoupledSoftmax + SoftTop-k
  - RAG application in Section C.9
  - Section 2 literature, Section 3 background, Sections 4 and 5 contributions

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Dual-encoder (DE) models have been very successful for dense retrieval in open-domain question answering (openQA) systems. Given a user's query, they retrieve the relevant passages or documents from a large corpus in an efficient way. They do this by mapping queries and documents into the same embedding space, so retrieval can be done with fast similarity search methods. One thing to note is that openQA benchmarks usually have multi-class training data (most queries have only one positive document) and the training data is limited (each document in the corpus has zero or very few tagged queries, i.e. a zero/few-shot scenario). So on these benchmarks the models have to generalize and retrieve relevant documents even if those documents might not have been in the training set.

There is another important retrieval scenario that comes up a lot in real-world applications like search engines and recommendation systems. Here we want to retrieve multiple documents/items from a large collection, and there are a significant number of seen examples per document/item, i.e., a many-shot scenario. These tasks are often formulated as extreme multi-label classification (XMC) tasks, where each document/item to be retrieved is treated as a separate label. XMC also shows up in newer applications such as retrieval augmented generation (RAG). When multiple documents could contain the desired answer, the retrieval task in RAG is very close to an XMC problem. XMC algorithms usually need to both “memorize” and “generalize”. For each label they need to memorize which types of queries are relevant. For example in product to product recommendation, the algorithm should memorize which products can lead to a click on a particular product, using the product-product co-click data that is provided. But at the same time the algorithm also has to generalize on unseen queries.

In the XMC community it is commonly believed that DE by themselves are not enough to get good performance, because of the semantic gap and the knowledge-intensive nature of XMC benchmarks. To overcome the semantic gap and enable memorization, state-of-the-art (SOTA) XMC methods add either per-label classifiers or auxiliary parameters to the DE. We test this belief with a simple experiment on a synthetic dataset. In this dataset a random query text is associated with a random document text, and the task is to memorize these random correlations during retrieval. We find that DE models can do this task with perfect accuracy, at least on datasets up to 1M scale (cf. Section C.1). This disputes the belief that was held before in the literature.

- Question: “Are pure DE models sufficient for XMC tasks?”
  - why pure DE: 1) parameter efficient, model size / trainable params don't scale linearly with #labels (Figure 1); 2) XMC needs re-training for new labels, DE generalize via features
  - pure DE match or beat SOTA XMC by up to 2% on largest public benchmarks, 20 \times smaller
  - key: right loss + extensive negatives (consistent, unbiased loss feedback); call it DEXML (Dual-Encoders for eXtreme Multi-Label classification)
- Losses and scaling
  - OvA-BCE doesn't train effectively, InfoNCE disincentivizes confident predictions
  - \mathsf{DecoupledSoftmax} (modified InfoNCE, removes correlation between positive labels); {\mathsf{SoftTop}\text{-k}} for prediction budget size (k)
  - long tail -> many highly relevant negatives -> study with all negatives first
  - memory-efficient distributed implementation, multiple GPUs, modified gradient cache, modest GPU setup (Table 1, 9)
  - approximations with hard negative mining
- Contributions: DE alone SOTA + unifies XMC and retrieval; existing losses inappropriate; DecoupledSoftmax and SoftTop-k; RAG task in Section C.9
- Roadmap: Section 2 literature, Section 3 background, Sections 4 and 5 contributions

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Dual-encoder (DE) models have been very successful for dense retrieval in open-domain question answering (openQA) systems. Given a user's query, they retrieve the relevant passages or documents from a large corpus in an efficient way. They do this by mapping queries and documents into the same embedding space, so retrieval can be done with fast similarity search methods. One thing to note is that openQA benchmarks usually have multi-class training data (most queries have only one positive document) and the training data is limited (each document in the corpus has zero or very few tagged queries, i.e. a zero/few-shot scenario). So on these benchmarks the models have to generalize and retrieve relevant documents even if those documents might not have been in the training set.

There is another important retrieval scenario that comes up a lot in real-world applications like search engines and recommendation systems. Here we want to retrieve multiple documents/items from a large collection, and there are a significant number of seen examples per document/item, i.e., a many-shot scenario. These tasks are often formulated as extreme multi-label classification (XMC) tasks, where each document/item to be retrieved is treated as a separate label. XMC also shows up in newer applications such as retrieval augmented generation (RAG). When multiple documents could contain the desired answer, the retrieval task in RAG is very close to an XMC problem. XMC algorithms usually need to both “memorize” and “generalize”. For each label they need to memorize which types of queries are relevant. For example in product to product recommendation, the algorithm should memorize which products can lead to a click on a particular product, using the product-product co-click data that is provided. But at the same time the algorithm also has to generalize on unseen queries.

In the XMC community it is commonly believed that DE by themselves are not enough to get good performance, because of the semantic gap and the knowledge-intensive nature of XMC benchmarks. To overcome the semantic gap and enable memorization, state-of-the-art (SOTA) XMC methods add either per-label classifiers or auxiliary parameters to the DE. We test this belief with a simple experiment on a synthetic dataset. In this dataset a random query text is associated with a random document text, and the task is to memorize these random correlations during retrieval. We find that DE models can do this task with perfect accuracy, at least on datasets up to 1M scale (cf. Section C.1). This disputes the belief that was held before in the literature.

Based on this synthetic experiment, this work tries to answer the question: “Are pure DE models sufficient for XMC tasks?” There are two reasons a pure DE model is desirable. 1) DE methods are parameter efficient, unlike XMC methods, i.e. the model size (and so the number of trainable parameters) does not scale linearly with the number of labels (see Figure 1). 2) XMC methods need re-training or model updates when they encounter new labels, while DE methods can generalize to new labels based on their features. Our work shows that pure DE models can actually match or even outperform SOTA XMC methods by up to 2%, even on the largest public XMC benchmarks, and they are 20 \times smaller in model size. What makes the performance better is the right loss formulation for the task and using extensive negatives so that the loss feedback is consistent and unbiased. We call DE models trained with our approach DEXML (Dual-Encoders for eXtreme Multi-Label classification).

First we analyze existing multi-label and contrastive training losses like One-versus-All Binary Cross-Entropy (OvA-BCE) and InfoNCE, and show how they may not be adequate for training dual-encoder models in XMC. OvA-BCE does not train effectively and InfoNCE disincentivizes confident predictions. To fix these limitations we propose a simple modification to the InfoNCE loss, the \mathsf{DecoupledSoftmax} loss, which removes the undesirable correlation between positive labels during training. We also extend the loss design to the {\mathsf{SoftTop}\text{-k}} loss, which is made to optimize prediction accuracy within a specific prediction budget size (k). This can be relevant for XMC applications where the goal is to make a fixed number of highly accurate predictions from a huge set of possible labels. Also, XMC problems have a long tail of labels, and at the query level this shows up as a large number of highly relevant negatives. So to establish the full potential of DE methods we first study our loss using all the negatives in the loss term. Of course including all negatives is hard for datasets with millions of labels. For this we provide a memory-efficient distributed implementation that can use multiple GPUs and a modified gradient cache approach, which scales DE training to the largest public XMC benchmarks even with a modest GPU setup (see Table 1, 9). We also study how the proposed loss functions perform when they are approximated with standard hard negative mining approaches, and what that implies. The contributions of this work are:

- We show that dual-encoder methods alone can get SOTA performance on XMC tasks, which gives a more parameter-efficient and generalizable approach for XMC. This also unifies the approaches for XMC and retrieval problems and could lead to simplified and universally applicable solutions.

- We analyze existing multi-label and contrastive training losses and show they are not appropriate for training dual-encoder models in XMC settings. OvA-BCE does not train effectively and InfoNCE disincentivizes confident predictions.

- We propose a simple modification to the InfoNCE loss, the \mathsf{DecoupledSoftmax} loss, which overcomes these limitations. We also extend it to the {\mathsf{SoftTop}\text{-k}} loss, which is tailored to optimize prediction accuracy within a specific prediction budget size.

- Lastly, we explore applying our proposed loss functions to an RAG task in Section C.9, which shows promise for our approach over standard encoder training in RAG.

We discuss relevant literature in Section 2 and introduce the necessary background in Section 3, and then give a detailed account of our contributions in Section 4 and 5.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Dual-encoder (DE) models have been highly successful in dense retrieval tasks for open-domain question answering (openQA) systems [1,2,3], where they efficiently retrieve relevant passages or documents from a large corpus given a user’s query. These models map both queries and documents into a shared embedding space, which enables efficient retrieval using fast similarity search methods [4,5]. Notably, openQA benchmarks are often characterized by multi-class (most queries are tagged with a single positive document) and limited (each document in the corpus has zero or very few tagged queries i.e. zero/few-shot scenario) training data. On these benchmarks, models are required to generalize and retrieve relevant documents even though those documents might not have appeared in the training set.

Another important retrieval scenario, which frequently arises in real-world applications such as search engines [6] and recommendation systems [7,8], is where we want to retrieve multiple documents/items from a large collection based on a significant number of seen examples per document/item, i.e., a many-shot scenario. Such tasks are often formulated as extreme multi-label classification (XMC) tasks, where each document/item to be retrieved is treated as a separate label [9]. XMC also appears in emerging applications such as retrieval augmented generation (RAG) [10]. In particular, when multiple documents can potentially contain the desired answer, the retrieval task in RAG closely aligns with an XMC problem. Typically, XMC algorithms need to both “memorize” and “generalize”: for each label they need to memorize the type of queries that are relevant; e.g., for a product to product recommendation scenario, the algorithm should memorize which products can lead to a click on a particular product using the provided product-product co-click data. At the same time, the algorithm should generalize on unseen queries.

It is a prevailing belief in the XMC community that, due to the semantic gap and knowledge-intensive nature of XMC benchmarks, DE by themselves are not sufficient to attain good performance [11]. To overcome the semantic gap and enable memorization, state-of-the-art (SOTA) XMC methods augment DE with either per-label classifiers [12,13] or auxiliary parameters [11]. We explore this belief with a simple experiment on a synthetic dataset where a random query text is associated with a random document text, and the task is to memorize these random correlations during retrieval. We find that DE models are able to perform this task with perfect accuracy at least on up to 1M scale datasets (cf. Section C.1), which disputes the belief previously held in the literature.

In light of this synthetic experiment, this work aims to answer the following question: “Are pure DE models sufficient for XMC tasks?” A pure DE model is desirable because: 1) unlike XMC methods, DE methods are parameter efficient, i.e. the model size (and consequently the number of trainable parameters) does not scale linearly with the number of labels (see Figure 1); 2) XMC methods require re-training or model updates when they encounter new labels, whereas DE methods can generalize to new labels based on their features. Interestingly, our work shows that pure DE models can indeed match or even outperform SOTA XMC methods by up to 2% even on the largest public XMC benchmarks while being 20 \times smaller in model size. The key to the improved performance is the right loss formulation for the underlying task and the use of extensive negatives to give consistent and unbiased loss feedback. We refer to DE models trained with the proposed approach as DEXML (Dual-Encoders for eXtreme Multi-Label classification).

We begin by analyzing existing multi-label and contrastive training losses like One-versus-All Binary Cross-Entropy (OvA-BCE) and InfoNCE, and highlight how they may be inadequate for training dual-encoder models in XMC. Specifically, OvA-BCE does not train effectively and InfoNCE disincentivizes confident predictions. To overcome these limitations, we propose a simple modification to the InfoNCE loss, the \mathsf{DecoupledSoftmax} loss, which removes the undesirable correlation between positive labels during training. We further extend our loss design to the {\mathsf{SoftTop}\text{-k}} loss, which is tailored to optimize prediction accuracy within a specific prediction budget size (k). This is particularly relevant to XMC applications where the goal is to make a fixed number of highly accurate predictions from a vast set of possible labels. Moreover, XMC problems involve a long tail of labels, which at the query level manifests as a large number of highly relevant negatives. To establish the full potential of DE methods, we therefore first study our proposed loss using all the negatives in the loss term. Naturally, including all negatives is challenging for million-label scale datasets, so we provide a memory-efficient distributed implementation that can use multiple GPUs and a modified gradient cache [14] approach to scale DE training to the largest public XMC benchmarks even with a modest GPU setup (see Table 1, 9). We further study the performance and implications of approximating the proposed loss functions using standard hard negative mining approaches. In summary, the contributions of this work include:

- • We demonstrate that dual-encoder methods alone can achieve SOTA performance on XMC tasks, leading to a more parameter-efficient and generalizable approach for XMC. This also unifies the approaches for XMC and retrieval problems, paving the way for simplified and universally applicable solutions.

- • We analyze existing multi-label and contrastive training losses and show they are not appropriate for training dual-encoder models in XMC settings. Specifically, OvA-BCE does not train effectively and InfoNCE disincentivizes confident predictions.

- • We propose a simple modification to the InfoNCE loss, namely the \mathsf{DecoupledSoftmax} loss, which overcomes these limitations. We further extend our loss design to the {\mathsf{SoftTop}\text{-k}} loss, which is tailored to optimize prediction accuracy within a specific prediction budget size.

- • Lastly, we explore applications of our proposed loss functions on an RAG task in Section C.9, which shows promise for our proposed approach over standard encoder training in RAG.

Before giving a detailed account of our contributions in Section 4 and 5, we discuss relevant literature in Section 2 and introduce the necessary background in Section 3.
